_provenance.note: North Dakota SNAP curated supplements. North Dakota has NO existing packages/snap-rules StatePolicy entry and NO oracle-fixture coverage — a genuine blank slate, matching this roster's prior blank-slate builds (Nebraska, Connecticut, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, New Hampshire). This pack is CORPUS-ONLY and does not touch packages/snap-rules or the oracle fixture. North Dakota is built as part of a five-agent parallel batch (RI, MT, DE, SD, ND) built concurrently by separate agents. Drafted from direct fetches of North Dakota HHS's CURRENT, actively-versioned SNAP policy manual (nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/SNAP/), cross-checked against the state's own Release Log dates and the USDA federal ABAWD-waiver and food-restriction-waiver trackers; a legacy, stale manual mirror at nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/43005/ was identified and explicitly NOT relied on for any current dollar figure or post-OBBBA eligibility rule.

terms: department of health and human services
supplements.citation: North Dakota HHS SNAP consumer/FAQ page (hhs.nd.gov/applyforhelp/snap); ND Self-Service Portal (dhsbenefits.dhs.nd.gov); North Dakota Century Code Chapter 50-01.1 (Human Service Zones)
supplements.heading: North Dakota calls its program plainly "SNAP" — no distinctive local brand — and delivers it through 19 state-supervised "Human Service Zones," a genuinely distinctive local structure created by a 2019 legislative restructuring
supplements.text: North Dakota HHS's own consumer materials use only the generic federal name "SNAP" — this pack found no distinctive North Dakota-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." Applicants can apply online through the ND Self-Service Portal (dhsbenefits.dhs.nd.gov/SSPPortal), request a mailed application through an HHS online form, or apply in person or by mail using Application for Assistance form SFN 405 (available in English and Spanish), submitted to their local Human Service Zone office. The Customer Support Center answers questions before and during the application process. North Dakota's SNAP program is administered by the state Department of Health and Human Services but DELIVERED locally through 19 Human Service Zones — a structure created by the 2019 Legislature's SB 2124 (North Dakota Century Code Chapter 50-01.1), which dissolved the prior 47 county-run social service offices (across the state's 53 counties) and re-formed them, effective January 1, 2020, into 19 mostly-multicounty zones, each administratively hosted by one lead county. This pack flags this Zone structure explicitly: North Dakota is neither a single centralized state office (like this roster's New Hampshire) nor a plain independent-county model (like this roster's California, New York, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Virginia) — it sits in between, with state policy supervision but zone-level day-to-day delivery, and this pack recommends confirming operative local practice with the applicant's own Human Service Zone office specifically.

supplements.citation: North Dakota HHS SNAP Manual § 505, Categorical and Broad Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE), revised 5/16/2025; § 601, Resources Overview, revised 5/16/2025; § 604, Vehicles; Policy Release 26.2 (Appendix B, effective 4/1/2026)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CORRECTION: North Dakota's current SNAP resource limit is $3,000 (all other households) / $4,500 (elderly or disabled households) — NOT the lower $2,250/$3,250 figures several secondary sources repeat
supplements.text: North Dakota runs a 200% FPG BBCE track (HHS's manual calls it interchangeably "BBCE (TANF I&R)" in § 505's narrative text and "Expanded Categorically Eligible (ECE)" in Appendix B's income tables — this pack treats these as the same pathway under two labels, not two separate tracks) alongside the federal-baseline 130% gross / 100% net income tests. Current FFY2026 (10/1/2025-9/30/2026) figures by household size 1: 200% ECE/BBCE gross limit $2,610; 130% gross limit $1,696; 165% gross limit (a federal baseline test used only when an elderly/disabled household member and others in the home purchase and prepare food separately) $2,152; 100% net limit $1,305 — each rising by a per-additional-member increment through household size 8 and beyond. A household passing the 200% BBCE/ECE track faces NO resource test at all. A household that has not established BBCE/ECE eligibility (or a BBCE/ECE household with an elderly/disabled member that fails the 200% test, which must then be re-tested under regular SNAP rules) faces a real, enforced resource limit: this pack fetched HHS's own current § 601 Resources Overview directly (revised 5/16/2025) and confirms $4,500 for households with an elderly or disabled member, $3,000 for all other households — this pack flags explicitly that this CORRECTS a lower $2,250/$3,250 figure repeated across multiple secondary SNAP-eligibility aggregator sites this pack found (povertylevelcalculator.com, snapbenefitshelp.com, and similar), which appear to reflect an older, un-updated figure. Vehicles: HHS's § 604 gives every licensed vehicle a flat $4,650 fair-market-value exclusion (vehicles above that equity value have only the excess counted as a resource); a genuinely North Dakota-specific rule this pack found directly in § 604's own text: "On Indian reservations that do not require vehicles driven by tribal members to be licensed, such vehicles must be treated as licensed vehicles" for this same $4,650 exclusion purpose — this pack flags this as a real, narrow, reservation-specific administrative accommodation rather than a general statement about tribal land.

supplements.citation: North Dakota Century Code § 50-06-05.1, effective 2017 — full opt-out of the federal drug-felony ban; North Dakota HHS SNAP Manual § 430-05-77-55, Other Disqualifications (legacy host; SNAP-trafficking-specific disqualifications only)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CONFIRMATION (of a minority-position claim): North Dakota FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban via state statute — this pack cross-checked the statute's own operative text against HHS's disqualification-rules text and found no conflicting general ban
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack treats a full opt-out as a genuine minority position among states nationally (most states this roster has built carry a MODIFIED ban, not a full opt-out) deserving primary-source confirmation rather than acceptance at face value. North Dakota Century Code § 50-06-05.1 states: "the department may not deny assistance under the supplemental nutrition assistance program to any individual who has been convicted of a felony offense that has as an element the possession, use, or distribution of a controlled substance" — a full opt-out, effective 2017 per secondary-source corroboration this pack found (Public Health Law Center's SNAP Ban Opt-Out States Map), which this pack did not independently fetch the enacting session-law citation for but treats the statutory text itself, quoted directly from the Public Health Law Center's page, as reliable. This pack cross-checked this claim against HHS's own SNAP manual disqualification-rules text (§ 430-05-77-55, Other Disqualifications) and found NO general drug-felony-conviction disqualification category at all — only SNAP-program-integrity-specific disqualifications: sale of a controlled substance INVOLVING SNAP BENEFITS (24 months first violation, permanent second violation), sale of firearms/ammunition/explosives involving SNAP benefits (permanent), fleeing-felon or parole/probation-violator status, and trafficking benefits for $500 or more (permanent) — this pack flags this absence as consistent with (not merely asserting) the statutory full-opt-out claim, and distinguishes these SNAP-trafficking-specific penalties explicitly from a general drug-felony-conviction ban so the two are not conflated. This pack did NOT independently fetch the current (post-2025-renumbering) version of this disqualifications section from the new SNAP/ manual host and flags this specific citation as legacy-host-sourced in freshness.json — the underlying statutory opt-out claim is unaffected by this gap, since it rests on the Century Code text itself, not the manual section.

supplements.citation: North Dakota HHS SNAP Policy Release 26.2 (Appendix B, Table of Standards, effective 4/1/2026); Policy Release 25.6 (Standard Deduction, effective 10/1/2025)
supplements.heading: North Dakota's Standard Utility Allowance recently increased to $775/month (from $772), effective 4/1/2026, mid-FFY2026 — a genuine within-cycle adjustment this pack flags explicitly since most states in this roster hold utility figures constant for a full fiscal year
supplements.text: North Dakota's Standard Deduction (per HHS's Policy Release 25.6, effective 10/1/2025, the start of FFY2026) is $209 for household sizes 1 through 3, $223 for size 4, $261 for size 5, and $299 for size 6 or more — matching the current national FFY2026 figures this roster's New Hampshire pack has also independently confirmed. North Dakota's utility-allowance structure has four tiers: the Standard Utility Allowance (SUA, for households with heating or cooling costs) increased from $772 to $775/month effective 4/1/2026 per Policy Release 26.2 — this pack flags this explicitly as a genuine MID-FISCAL-YEAR adjustment, distinct from most states in this roster where the SUA figure holds constant for the full October-to-September fiscal year; the Limited Utility Allowance (LUSA, for two or more qualifying non-heating utility costs) is $286; the Minimum Utility Standard (MU, for one qualifying utility cost) is $126; and the Telephone Standard (telephone-only) is $35. The Maximum Shelter Deduction (excess-shelter cap for households without an elderly/disabled member) is $744/month, and the Homeless Shelter Deduction is $198.99/month — both matching the current national FFY2026 figures this roster's other states have confirmed. This pack separately found, via HHS's own dated Release Log (Release 25.8, effective 11/13/2025), that North Dakota restricted the automatic SUA-eligibility trigger tied to a LIHEAP payment to households with an elderly or disabled member only — this pack did NOT independently fetch the full current § 803 Shelter Deductions section text and flags this specific LIHEAP-trigger restriction as Release-Log-summary-sourced only, not independently confirmed against the underlying section's full current text, in freshness.json.

supplements.citation: North Dakota HHS SNAP Policy Release 25.7 (effective 11/1/2025, amended 11/13/2025); USDA FNS/FNA ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index (no FY2026 North Dakota entry)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CORRECTION: North Dakota's ABAWD Rolette County / Turtle Mountain Reservation geographic waiver ENDED effective 10/31/2025 and was not renewed — contradicting a secondary-source claim of an active statewide waiver through mid-2026
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched North Dakota HHS's own Policy Release 25.7 (effective 11/1/2025, amended 11/13/2025) directly and confirms the current, post-OBBBA rules: the ABAWD age range is 18 through 64 (an individual is no longer considered an ABAWD the month they turn 65, and the exemption for turning 65 begins the first of that month); the child-in-household exemption threshold decreased from under-18 to under-14; a NEW exemption was added for "Indians, Urban Indians, or California Indians" — defined by HHS as people eligible for Indian Health Service (IHS), including members and descendants of federally recognized American Indian or Alaska Native tribes plus California Indians and others recognized under federal law, with verification required — this pack flags this as the ABAWD-specific answer to this pack's tribal/reservation disclosure requirement, distinct from the separate reservation-specific vehicle-licensing rule (income-and-resources supplement) and Food Distribution Program choice-of-program rules (tribal-programs supplement). Release 25.7's summary text states the OBBBA rollout also removed the blanket Veteran, Homeless, and Former Foster Care exemptions nationally; this pack notes the release document's own detailed redline body text still shows these three exemption categories listed in a way that reads ambiguously (likely reflecting lost strikethrough formatting from the source PDF's tracked-changes format) — this pack resolves the ambiguity in favor of the release's own explicit summary line ("Removal of exemptions for Veterans, Homeless and Former Foster Care"), consistent with the nationwide OBBBA rollout this roster's other 2025-2026-built packs have documented, but flags this specific resolution as based on the summary line rather than an unambiguous read of the body text. THE FLAGSHIP FINDING: this same Release 25.7 states explicitly that North Dakota's ABAWD Geographic Waiver — which had covered the Turtle Mountain Reservation and Rolette County under a prior 7/1/2025-6/30/2026 waiver period — was ENDING effective 10/31/2025, with affected individuals mailed notice on 10/10/2025 informing them they would need to meet the new Indians/Urban Indians/California Indians exemption or another exemption to remain exempt. This pack cross-checked this directly against USDA FNS/FNA's own ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index, which lists North Dakota's most recent posted waiver-response entry as FY2025 (dated 6/18/2025) with NO FY2026 entry — corroborating that no waiver was renewed. This pack found and explicitly CORRECTS a WebSearch-surfaced secondary-source claim (an aggregator site) stating North Dakota "holds an active statewide waiver through June 30, 2026" — this pack's primary-source reading, confirmed by both HHS's own dated release document and USDA's own tracker, is that North Dakota currently has NO active ABAWD geographic waiver anywhere in the state as of 11/1/2025 onward, through at least this pack's research date (Release Log entries through 26.5, dated 6/15/2026, show no further update to § 403 Geographic Waiver).

supplements.citation: USDA FNS/FNA approval letter, North Dakota SNAP Food Restriction Waiver Demonstration Project, Secretary Brooke Rollins, dated 12/10/2025, effective 9/1/2026
supplements.heading: TIME-SENSITIVE FLAGSHIP FINDING: North Dakota excludes soft drinks, energy drinks, and candy from SNAP-eligible purchases — IN EFFECT since September 1, 2026
supplements.text: North Dakota is one of a small handful of states (alongside, per this pack's WebSearch corroboration, Hawaii, Missouri, South Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee in the same USDA approval round) that requested and received a novel USDA demonstration-project waiver amending the statutory federal definition of "food" for SNAP purchasing purposes within the state. This pack fetched USDA FNS's own approval letter directly: Secretary Brooke Rollins approved North Dakota HHS's request (submitted 10/24/2025, revised 11/3/2025) on December 10, 2025, to exclude soft drinks, energy drinks, and candy from SNAP-purchasable food, for a 2-year pilot period (extendable by up to three additional 1-year extensions upon request), EFFECTIVE SEPTEMBER 1, 2026. That date has now passed: as of 9/1/2026 the restriction is IN EFFECT, so an applicant in North Dakota can no longer buy candy, soft drinks, or energy drinks with SNAP benefits. This pack did not independently fetch the full Terms and Conditions PDF defining exactly which specific products count as "candy" or "energy drinks" under the waiver (the underlying federal statutory definitions at 7 U.S.C. § 2012(k) generally hinge on flour content for candy and a "Supplement Facts" label for energy/nutrition-labeled beverages) and flags this level of product-category granularity as a genuine research gap in freshness.json — a future pass, especially close to or after 9/1/2026, should fetch the Terms and Conditions PDF directly for exact product-category boundaries.

supplements.citation: North Dakota HHS Apply for Help — SNAP FAQ page (explicit list of non-purchasable items, including hot prepared foods); WebSearch corroboration (Propel state EBT guide)
supplements.heading: North Dakota does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. This pack found consistent corroboration across HHS's own consumer FAQ page (which explicitly lists "food that will be eaten in the store" and "foods that are hot at the point of sale" among items households CANNOT buy with SNAP benefits) and secondary-source corroboration (Propel's state EBT guide) that North Dakota does NOT currently operate an RMP. This pack found no pending North Dakota legislation analogous to other states' RMP-establishment bills. North Dakota's operative answer for an applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at a restaurant is a plain no — EBT purchases are limited to grocery-style food for home preparation and consumption, with the standard federal exceptions for seeds and plants that produce food.

supplements.citation: North Dakota HHS SNAP Manual (legacy host), Food Distribution (Tribal Commodities) Program Information Sharing § 430-05-05-50, and Choice of SNAP or Food Distribution Program § 430-05-05-50-05
supplements.heading: North Dakota households on or near reservations may choose SNAP OR the Food Distribution Program (Commodities/FDPIR), but not both simultaneously — this pack found no other tribal/reservation-specific SNAP administrative structure beyond this choice-of-program rule and a narrow vehicle-licensing accommodation
supplements.text: North Dakota has multiple federally recognized tribal nations with reservation land (Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, Spirit Lake Tribe, Three Affiliated Tribes/MHA Nation at Fort Berthold, and the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate straddling the North Dakota/South Dakota border). This pack researched specifically for any North Dakota-specific SNAP manual notes on FDPIR interaction or reservation-specific administration and found: households on or near a reservation may participate in EITHER SNAP OR the Food Distribution Program (Commodities, the state/tribal implementation of the federal FDPIR), but never both in the same month — dual participation triggers a claim. A household may switch between the two programs only at the end of its current review/certification period, or by voluntarily terminating one program and applying fresh for the other (eligibility for the new program begins the month AFTER the prior program's termination, per HHS's own worked example). An individual disqualified from SNAP for an Intentional Program Violation (IPV) or court conviction of fraud may not participate in the Food Distribution Program until the SNAP disqualification period expires, and the reverse also holds (a Food Distribution Program IPV disqualification blocks SNAP participation for the same period) — but an individual disqualified from SNAP for a reason OTHER than IPV/fraud may still be eligible for the Food Distribution Program. This pack separately found one narrow, genuinely reservation-specific administrative rule in HHS's Vehicles section (§ 604): "On Indian reservations that do not require vehicles driven by tribal members to be licensed, such vehicles must be treated as licensed vehicles" for SNAP resource-valuation purposes (see income-and-resources supplement) — but this pack found NO evidence of a broader reservation-specific SNAP administrative structure, no distinct application process, and no separate income/resource standard for reservation residents beyond these two rules. This pack discloses explicitly that it did NOT independently fetch the current (post-2025-renumbering) version of this Food Distribution Program section from the new SNAP/ manual host and relied on the legacy 43005 host for this specific topic, flagged in freshness.json, because this content describes a longstanding structural choice-of-program rule that this pack judged less likely to have changed in the 2025 renumbering than dollar figures or OBBBA-driven eligibility criteria — but this judgment call itself should be re-verified against the current host before being treated as settled.
